5 Famous Car Nameplates Resurrected by Boring Crossovers
57 photos
Photo: Ford
A cool name is one of the most important details that make a car become a lovable piece of automotive history, so it’s arguably worth more than most people realize. It takes decades and millions of devoted fans to build a car name that starts to truly mean something.
This is why iconic cars like the Mustang , the 911, the Corvette or the G-Wagen don’t really need explanatory commercials, and sometimes they don’t even need an introduction. People already know them by associating their name with what they managed to represent during their existence.
It’s also why carmakers have started digging up cool nameplates for some of their modern lineups, and most of these revivals are honestly honoring the originals. I mean, look at the latest Renault 5 , which came as an electric hatchback that looks and even feels like a modern answer to the original. The Ford Bronco is another good example, as it’s a boxy and capable off-roader that its ancestors would definitely recognize, despite the fact that it has no V8 option.
Heck, you could say that the entire MINI lineup is a tribute to the original Mini, and there are plenty of other examples of nameplate revival done right. Unfortunately, over the years there have also been some pretty poor examples of the sort, where a famous badge from a coupe, a sports car, or any other cult favorite has been desecrated by being put on something that has almost no connection to the original.
In fact, in recent years there have been tons of examples of new cars that are usually crossovers, built on a shared FWD-based platform, and simply designed to look trendy and sell in large numbers to sensible buyers who don’t really care about the history of their car’s nameplate.
There is obviously nothing wrong with those cars or those customers, but I think there is a huge problem with calling that vehicle something that it clearly isn’t. Sadly, these kinds of examples have begun to multiply in recent years, which is why I decided to bring the most notorious ones together in this article.
I didn’t try to do a “name and shame” piece, but the following is not far from one either. I do understand the logic behind what the following carmakers are doing, and it’s obvious mostly working out for them. If you launch a brand new car you usually need to invest in a nameplate a bit more than just a few extra brainstorming hours from the marketing department.
After being introduced, a new name has to be explained and repeated until it sticks by hopefully making a good impression. That takes a lot of money and especially time, and it’s also a lottery, as some people might overlook a new car simply because its name doesn’t resonate with them.
On the other hand, an old name, especially from an iconic model, already has recognition, and it also comes pre-packed with a bit of emotion. Reusing it on an otherwise forgettable or mainstream new vehicle is a recipe for attention, especially in a crowded market where most crossovers look and drive like each other.
That said, I firmly believe that attaching a name from an old iconic model to something that has almost nothing in common with the original makes it lose a bit of its charm, and more of its weight. For example, the next generation of buyers will only know the Ford Capri as an electric crossover built on a Volkswagen platform, not as the lovable and iconic “ European Mustang. ”
With that in mind, I decided to have a look at all the revived nameplates in recent years that have strayed the most from their origins. Each of the following cars wears a famous badge, and each one has almost nothing in common with the vehicle that made that badge famous in the first place.
Mitsubishi Eclipse Cross and Eclipse Sportback: From Street Racer to Benign Crossovers For an entire generation of especially American sports car enthusiasts, the Mitsubishi Eclipse was a rather affordable way of entering the world of fast Japanese cars. Mitsubishi sold over 1.4 million units across four generations until 2012, with early cars being built in Illinois by Diamond-Star Motors, a joint-venture with Chrysler that also built the Eagle Talon and Plymouth Laser.
Photo: Mitsubishi By far the most loved versions were the turbocharged AWD Eclipses, which also became tuner favorites. A late example Eclipse even had a role in the Fast & furious films, turning it into a pop culture icon. Later generations did grow softer, heavier and FWD-only, and the last one left the production line in 2012, but they were still seen as entry-level sports cars.
Fast forward about five years, and the Eclipse name returned at the 2017 Geneva Motor show, where Mitsubishi presented the Eclipse Cross, a compact crossover slotting between the ASX and the Outlander, built on an existing platform. With a 1.5-liter four-cylinder that was usually paired with a CVT, the somewhat competent but otherwise unremarkable crossover wasn’t exactly making fans of the original Eclipse proud.
What happened after took the famous badge even further away from its origins, as in a few years the Eclipse Cross name started appearing in Europe on a subcompact crossover that was essentially a Renault Scenic E-Tech. Apart from the name, the model had absolutely nothing in common with any Mitsubishi whatsoever.
Photo: Mitsubishi Complicating things even further, North America also saw Mitsubishi applying the Eclipse name on a re-badged Nissan Leaf starting with 2026. In other words, what originally started as an inexpensive sporty coupe that received a lot of love in the tuning scene, ended up as a crossover, a French electric car and an American-market electric Nissan.
Chevrolet Blazer: Close Tribute, But Definitely No Cigar Out of all the funky nameplate revivals on this list, the Chevrolet Blazer is probably the easiest to understand, since it was an SUV name that was essentially resurrected by a crossover. That said, it’s still pretty hilarious how small is the resemblance between the old and the new when you compare them,
Photo: Chevrolet The original was introduced in 1969 as the K5 Blazer, and it was developed to take on off-roaders like the Ford Bronco, the International Scout and the Jeep Wrangler’s predecessor. Chevrolet had simply shortened its full-size C/K pickup truck chassis, keeping the body-on-frame chassis, live axles, and part-time four-wheel-drive, while adding the option of a fiberglass roof that could be removed.
In the beginning, the K5 Blazer was 4WD-only, and its engine lineup also included two V8s as range-topping versions. In 1983 it was joined by the S-10 Blazer, which used the compact S-10 pickup truck as its base, and for a while they were two differently sized Blazer that competed for two ends of the market.
Photo: Chevrolet Both were body-on-frame SUVs with 4WD, but starting with 1995 the big K5 Blazer was renamed the Tahoe, and the smaller S-10 was the only one remaining in production until 2005. Fast forward to 2018, and the Blazer name returned, only this time it was on a FWD-based crossover.
There was no more removable roof or hardcore 4WD system, albeit the new model was reasonably successful by providing exactly what the modern market wanted. Essentially a compact family crossover with Camaro-inspired exterior styling and plenty of creature comforts, the revived Blazer has almost nothing in common with the original, especially since it was eventually accompanied by the electric Blazer EV.
Ford Puma: The Sporty Subcompact Coupe That Became a Crossover The original Ford Puma is remembered by some as having one of the coolest launches for a small car ever. Leading its marketing plan was a TV advert that used digitally altered footage of Steve McQueen’s character from Bullitt, driving the little Puma coupe around San Francisco and then parking it in his garage next to the green Mustang and his motorcycle from The Great Escape.
Photo: Ford The model was a quirky-looking subcompact two-door built on the Ford Fiesta platform, sporting a 1.7-liter co-developed with Yamaha. The original Puma was the second Ford to sport the “New Edge” design introduced by the Ford Ka, and despite its less-than-premium underpinnings it was met with quite a great deal of respect by fans of small and inexpensive driver’s cars.
Introduced in 1997 specifically for the European market, it stayed part of Ford’s lineup until 2002, when a direct successor was no longer made. Fast forward seventeen year later, though, and Ford suddenly remembered that army of fans that the original Puma had amassed, and brought the nameplate out again.
This time, the new Puma is still based on the now-extinct Fiesta, but that is where the similarities ended. The new model was a five-door crossover aimed at the Nissan Juke, Renault Captur, and maybe the Volkswagen T-Cross, three city warriors that had completely cornered this part of the city car market.
Photo: Ford It’s only fair to admit that the second iteration of the Puma nameplate wasn’t put on a terrible car, but on the contrary, with sales definitely proving that. While the original was one of the most successful sporty cars in Europe, with over 130,000 units being sold in total, the new Ford Puma has already outsold it almost ten times. In other words, its success is probably not just thanks to wearing a famous name, but its customers are definitely not in the same category as fans of the original.
Chevrolet Trailblazer: From a Real SUV to a Three-Cylinder Grocery-Getter While the Blazer above at least somewhat kept its place in the middle of the Chevrolet range, the Trailblazer nameplate seriously moved down the ranks after its reintroduction. As its name suggests, the original first appeared as a trim level for the S-10 Blazer, and then it quickly became its own model.
Photo: Chevrolet It was a proper truck-based SUV, with body-on-frame construction and the option of 4WD with low range. In 2006 it even got an SS version, which paired a 6.0-liter LS2 V8 from the Corvette with a lowered and sports-tuned chassis and better brakes. That was a boxy SUV that could keep up with thoroughbred sports cars on the highway long before the AMG G-Wagen earned its place in this niche ecosystem.
When the Trailblazer name returned in 2019, it was on a subcompact crossovers developed and built by GM South Korea. This time, the model was positioned between the even smaller Trax and the Equinox, with a three-cylinder 1.2-liter under the hood with either FWD or AWD.
Apart from the name, there is absolutely nothing that connects it to the original model. There is no body-on-frame construction, no low-range gearbox, no six-cylinder and definitely no V8. In fact, its engine is half the size of the old base unit. It’s an entirely different car that arguably has the wrong name.
Photo: Chevrolet That said, the new Trailblazer found plenty of buyers, albeit most of them were only looking for an affordable and somewhat roomy small crossover with a reasonably interior equipment level. From that perspective, Chevrolet could have called it anything else but a Trailblazer.
Ford Capri: The 1970s Coupe You Always Promised Yourself, Revived as a VV Crossover If the previous cars on this list were more or less annoying for using the names of old vehicles that have very few things in common with them, the Ford Capri is probably the poster child for this weird marketing method. Even more sad, it doesn’t even seem to work.
Photo: Ford The original Ford Capri was unveiled back in the cool year of 1969, and many people saw it as the European Mustang. It was a long-hooded, short-tailed coupe built on the more humble Cortinas platform and had a more than reasonable pricing scheme. It was an immediate hit, with about 400,000 units being sold in the first two years of production, and it ran for three generations.
Comprising all kinds of powertrains, including the much-loved RS homologation specials, the Ford Capri is one of the coolest European-only Fords from the 1970s. When Ford decided to revive the nameplate in 2024, all that aura pretty much went down the drain, though.
Instead of an inexpensive RWD coupe that could stand up to cars like the BMW 2 Series Coupe or the Toyota Supra Mk 5, the new Capri is an electric coupe-crossover. Apart from the name, the only thing it has in common with the original model is the fact that it’s still built in Cologne, where many of the first Capris were also built.
Photo: Ford Technically, the new Capri is a fancier and less practical version of the Ford Explorer EV, which shares its platform and production line, with both models essentially being a redesigned Volkswagen ID.5 and ID.4, subsequently. In other words, the new Capri is not only radically different from its predecessor, but it’s not even a real Ford, since it uses VW’s MEB platform.
Just because this strategy somewhat worked with the Mustang Mach-E, it doesn't mean Ford should keep using it. What's next, a front-wheel-drive Ford Thunderbird grocery getter?

Aggressive Alfa Romeo GT Competizione Stems From Across Imagination Land, Dares For CGI Greatness
8 photos
Photo: my_vision_official / Instagram
Right now, everyone across the Internet is thinking about the latest Honda recalls or about the Ram recalls, plus the Tesla stock price and truck accident lawyers, when it comes to the automotive world.
Alas, some people look into the future – usually we would call them visionaries. But when it comes to the automotive realm, we just say they’re the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI. Poetic license, you know…
Anyway, one of these fine people has turned their CGI pen toward Alfa Romeo . The premium Italian automaker, which is a subsidiary of Stellantis (which recently announced it is abandoning motorsport outside America to cut costs), hasn’t done much lately – according to the FastLane 2030 recovery plan, it has become a regional rather than global brand.
To showcase its new place, during the recent 2026 Paris Motor Show in France, the brand, together with many of its cousins, has showcased both the current range of models, which consists of the very old Giulia and Stelvio plus the newer Tonale crossover SUV and the new best-selling Junior entry-level CUV, as well as a very cool prototype car.
The Alfa Romeo Cuorerosso concept was one of the big surprises of this year’s edition of the Mondial de l’Auto, a gorgeous four-door V6 creation that’s equally fashionable and impossible to put into production in this day and age. Luckily, there’s no need to bring it to life – it simply represents Alfa's new design language and the continuation of the Quadrifoglio's twin-turbo V6 legacy.
It has four doors, four seats, and a real engine under the hood, plus it shows a future with fewer giant screens in cars and more physical controls, as well as a potential for a multi-energy approach with hybrid, PHEV, and even all-electric applications. Anyway, that certainly gave people the courage to hope for the better for Alfa Romeo.
And the pixel masters didn’t hesitate – for example, the virtual artist known on the Internet only as My Vision, aka ' my_vision_official ,' has cooked up a spectacular but unofficial Alfa Romeo design project. It’s now influenced by the Cuorerosso except for the shared crimson hue – but it’s another statement of daringness for the ailing Italian brand.
More precisely, we are dealing here with the Alfa Romeo GT Competizione prototype, an unofficial, hypothetical design project featuring a compact three-door 2+2 coupe in the style of the Alfa Romeo Brera, but with a decidedly angular design and a raked rear that ends with a complete ducktail. It also has a ‘beak’ at the front personifying the classic ‘scudetto,’ along with massive wheels, humongous fender flares at the rear, and circular LED taillights plus stacked central exhaust outlets! By Angelo Mathais India correspondent
24 November 2026
The China-Persian Gulf corridor is poised for a container capacity boom as carriers eye sustained growth opportunities in an increasingly volatile trade environment, market updates suggest.
CULines is reportedly preparing a major network expansion programme for the tradelane, riding on the strength of a strategic partnership recently concluded with port operator Gulftainer for priority operating rights at the UAE’s Khor Fakkan Port.
Alongside Fujairah in the UAE and Sohar in Oman, Khor Fakkan has become a key Gulf bypass port, offering a lifeline of cargo flowing into the Middle East.
Sources say the Chinese carrier will deploy three large box ships from its fleet on the China-Gulf trade, marking a watershed moment in its service offerings.
“Two ships similar to the 10,100 teu Express Berlin in size will be added,” one industry source told The Loadstar . The Danaos-owned vessel previously operated by Sealead has been chartered by CULInes.
“Combined tonnage will be substantial for cargo connecting China and the Gulf,” the source added.
Earlier this year, CULines launched the China-Gulf Express (CGX) service with a rotation of Qingdao-Ningbo-Shekou-Nansha-Port Klang-Khor Fakkan, on which the Express Berlin is currently deployed.
Khor Fakkan has been operating under severe capacity strain, on- and off-dock, because of vessel call spikes tying up deployed industry capacity due to longer rotation cycles.
Vessel berthing/turnaround reliability through the priority handling partnership with Khor Fakkan operator Gulftainer is expected to fix those hurdles for CULines vessels calling at the contingency gateway, industry sources believe.
“This partnership marks an important milestone for Khor Fakkan, with long-term volume commitments and strengthening its position as a strategic gateway connecting Asia to the UAE and the wider Gulf,” said Gulftainer. “Beyond port access, our shared ambition is to develop an integrated trade corridor, leveraging Gulftainer’s continued investments in Khor Fakkan, inland dry ports and logistics infrastructure across Sharjah.”
CULines is not alone in rushing to field more capacity into the China-Khor Fakkan route.
Gulftainer’s container shipping arm, GT Lines, has also just set up a strategic vessel-sharing agreement with three budding Chinese container lines: Zhonggu Logistics; Sea Legend Shipping; and Ningbo Ocean Shipping.
The partners indicated they had plans to deploy five ships. two from GT Lines, to provide an upgraded Khor Fakkan-China Express 1 (KCX1) loop, with a 10-day sailing frequency they claimed would offer transit times of 18 days ex-South China, and 22 days ex-Central China, to Khor Fakkan.
“Through Gulftainer’s integrated logistics ecosystem, we provide seamless onward connectivity to the UAE, GCC [Gulf Cooperation Council] and Iraq, leveraging from our Khor Fakkan-Sharjah corridor,” said GT Lines.
These strategic collaborations are especially significant because Khor Fakkan, Fujairah, and Sohar all continue to struggle with major delays and congestion, according to Kuehne + Nagel’s Seaexplorer platform, with vessels waiting for up to a week for a berth, while delays for inland container transfers can be even higher, often running up to 15 days.

Google Maps Gets a Surprising Feature on Android Auto, What About Truck Navigation?
7 photos
Photo: Google
The number one feature - as in the one people use the most - in Google Maps is undoubtedly the navigation engine. And most people who use this feature drive a car, as Google Maps has become a must-have companion to go places in both familiar and unfamiliar regions.
While driving navigation is the number one feature, Google Maps can also offer turn-by-turn directions for cycling, walking, and public transportation when the app runs on a mobile device.
On Android Auto, the app defaults to driving for obvious reasons. This is about to change, according to a recent experiment quietly started by Google.
It looks like the search giant has brought motorcycle navigation to Google Maps on Android Auto, offering routes that are specifically tailored for two-wheelers.
This isn’t a feature that’s now available to all users, as Google has reportedly enabled it only on a very limited number of devices. The number of users running Android Auto on motorcycles is also quite small, considering not all models come with large screens to run Google’s app, so it’s not surprising that only a few people got the feature in the first place.
The first user who spotted the new feature was running Google Maps on Android Auto via Open Headunit. This is an application that allows an Android phone to double as an Android Auto screen, and considering their motorcycle did not have factory-installed Android Auto, this was a pretty convenient solution.
When launching Google Maps and searching for a route, they were provided with a notification to switch to “two-wheeler directions,” as the application somehow knew that routes tailored for motorcycles were required. When a suggested route was enabled, Google Maps started showing turn-by-turn directions alongside a motorcycle icon in the journey information panel.
Photo: reddit via AndroidAuthority Interestingly, the route Google Maps provided as part of this mode included shortcuts and narrow roads where a regular passenger vehicle wouldn’t fit. While this approach looks similar to cycling navigation - and it wouldn’t be such a big surprise for this feature to actually be the turn-by-turn navigation system aimed at bicycles - Google Maps automatically suggesting this mode is a sign that Google is cooking something.
Not everybody is getting this feature, and more importantly, it’s unclear who receives it and who doesn’t. On the other hand, it looks like Google is at least planning a navigation app - if not a motorcycle navigation mode entirely - and for the time being, waiting to see what happens is pretty much the only option. The future Google Maps beta builds could provide us with more details, as Google typically hides evidence of upcoming features in testing releases.
Truck navigation in Google Maps While this feature brings Google Maps closer to a new navigation mode, many people are still waiting for the search giant to update the application with turn-by-turn directions for large vehicles, such as motorhomes and lorries.
Just like in the case of motorcycle navigation, where Google Maps can look for more routes that aren’t always suitable for passenger vehicles, a truck navigation engine would have to consider vehicle dimensions and cargo size.
With such a system, Google Maps can offer routes specifically tailored for large vehicles, taking into account restrictions, limits, and eventually look for roads only where a vehicle can fit and is allowed to drive.
It’s no secret that many lorry drivers rely on Google Maps to find their destinations, and because the application doesn’t offer a route optimized for their vehicles, they end up stuck on narrow roads or in places where they can’t pass a bridge due to the size of their vehicles.
Photo: Google Google has so far ignored calls for a truck navigation update in Google Maps , and despite some signs that such a feature would eventually land in the application, no progress is believed to have been made on this front. Meanwhile, other applications, such as Sygic’s, continue to serve as reliable solutions for people who need navigation in large vehicles.
Google Maps is getting a ton of new features these days, including the immersive navigation update announced earlier this year and now rolling out to users in the United States. With immersive navigation, Google Maps adopts more detailed maps that include crosswalks, trees, 3D buildings, and see-through overpasses, making navigation more convenient for all users.
The feature is currently available only in the United States and Canada, though not even all users in these regions are getting it. Preparing the new maps for the public rollout takes time, and Google seemingly isn’t ready to reach broad availability.
The immersive navigation update will also go live on Android Auto once it’s ready for your device, and it won’t be tied to a specific app version. However, users are still recommended to keep the app up-to-date, not necessarily for new features, but also to receive the latest improvements and bug fixes once they go live. In the world of Android Auto, this is critical business, as bugs here have become painfully common.

Chevy Corvette ZR1 Takes On the Lambo Revuelto and the Porsche 911 Turbo S. The Winner Takes It All
23 photos
Photo: Carwow | YouTube
Three heavy-hitters, an American twin-turbo V8 brute, an Italian V12 plug-in hybrid exotic, and a German all-wheel-drive launch master, just lined up on the drag strip to settle an old-school debate: raw rear-wheel-drive horsepower versus electrified all-wheel-drive grip.
The Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 was General Motors’ fastest and most powerful Corvette until the ZR1X came along. Its 5.5-liter twin-turbocharged flat-plane-crank V8 (LT7) pumps out 1,064 horsepower (1,079 metric horsepower) and 828 pound-feet (1,123 Newton meters) of torque.
That is enough to make the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 2.3 seconds, run the quarter mile in 9.6 seconds with a trap speed of 150 mph (241 kph), and max out at 233 mph (375 kph). The eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure Corvette fashion with no electrification.
The Lamborghini Revuelto is the Italian house’s first plug-in hybrid. It rolls off the production line in Sant’Agata Bolognese with a V12 with naturally aspirated firepower and three electric motors for a combined output of 1,001 horsepower (1,015 metric horsepower) and 783 pound-feet (1,062 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Carwow | YouTube That is what makes it flash from 0 to 60 mph in 2.2 seconds, down the quarter mile in 9.4 seconds with a trap speed of 148 mph (238 kph), on its way to a top speed of 217 mph (350 kph). An eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners.
And then, there is the Porsche 911 Turbo S (992.2) with its 3.6-liter twin-turbocharged flat-six, working alongside an electric motor integrated into the transmission, producing 701 horsepower (711 metric horsepower) and 590 pound-feet (800 Newton meters) of torque.
The setup makes it accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in 2.4 seconds, run the quarter mile in just 9.9 seconds with a trap speed of 136 mph (219 kph), and go all the way to 200 mph (322 kph). An eight-speed PDK dual-clutch automatic transmission manages the power, throwing it to the pavement in an all-wheel-drive setup.
The Porsche is the lightest of the three at 3,829 pounds (1,737 kilograms). The C8 Chevy Corvette ZR1 tips the scales at 3,831 pounds (1,738 kilograms), while the Lamborghini Revuelto, with its plug-in hybrid system, weighs 4,072 pounds (1,847 kilograms).
On paper, everything seems clear when it comes to power. But how will it be on the drag strip? Mat Watson of Carwow took the trio to the track to determine the absolute king of the hill in a straight line. However, we have a plot twist. The Revuelto has a Mansory body kit. That is what Mat is driving.
Photo: Carwow | YouTube
On the first pass, the Lamborghini Revuelto gets off the line with the force of its 1,001 horsepower, and only the Porsche 911 Turbo S seems able to keep up with it, while the Corvette stays behind. But then, the ‘Vette closes in on the Porsche and overtakes it, but the Revuelto is the one to cross the finish line first.
The roll race puts them side by side at 50 mph (80 kph) before the drivers floor it. While Mat expects to win again, the 911 Turbo S launches like a rocket. Then comes the ZR1 and overtakes the Revuelto to claim second place once again, leaving the Revuelto at the back of the pack.
They run again, but this time launching at 40 mph (64 kph) in second gear and manual mode. This time, the Corvette puts its best “foot” forward and shoots ahead for the win, leaving the other two drivers scratching their heads. After all, it's the most powerful of the trio, so it has a reputation to uphold.
But will it work in a new roll race starting at 10 mph (16 kph) in first gear? Things seem to work in the Corvette ZR1’s favor once again. The Porsche 911 Turbo S is on its tail, while this time, the V12-powered plug-in hybrid Revuelto sits at the back of the pack.
Photo: Carwow | YouTube The trio tries a standard drag race from a standstill, and the three go head to head until the Corvette gains momentum and shoots ahead like no tomorrow for one more win. The Revuelto comes second, ahead of the Porsche, by a nose.
On another pass, something goes wrong with the Corvette, and it loses traction and precious time, giving the Porsche 911 Turbo S the chance to snatch its first win at the strip. The ZR1 and the Revuelto are in for a photo finish.
In the deciding drag race, the Corvette needs a bit of time to return to the lead right when Mat was hoping to win after his best start so far. The Porsche is second, and the Revuelto comes in third.
So the most powerful of the trio, the Corvette ZR1, only a tiny bit heavier than the Porsche, is the absolute winner, even though it got off to a bad start.

The US automaker is taking care of the Ford Ranger on the Old Continent with a new special edition dubbed Wolftrak that is arriving in early 2027 for both diesel and plug-in hybrid models.
The Ford Motor Company has been pretty busy lately: they just got into the spacecraft manufacturing business after recently becoming a battery cell manufacturer by purchasing a stake in Revolution Space. They are also targeting Japanese customers with the Ford Ranger, F-150, and Super Duty pickup trucks.
Over in Australia, their workhorse Ford Ranger Super Duty just got a railway pass with the Hy-Rail conversion, and on the Old Continent the latest Blue Oval news is also about the Ford Ranger – the regular one, not the Super Duty . More precisely, the local subsidiary of the US automaker is launching a new special edition called Ford Ranger Wolftrak that is ready for both “work and play.”
According to the company and Samir Jusupovic, who is Ranger’s brand manager in Europe , the new limited series 2027 Ford Ranger Wolftrak “pairs bold, off-road-inspired styling and a more refined cabin with the real-world capability expected of an International Pick-Up Award winner and Europe’s best-selling pickup for the past 11 consecutive years.”

We haven’t received great news from Stellantis recently – while Dodge and Ram are getting back into the NASCAR game, the European brands are abandoning motorsport entries : Peugeot quits the World Endurance Championship and Opel plus Citroen are pulling out of Formula E.
The group said that it will redirect the freed motorsport resources toward other things like customer racing and the creation of additional performance-oriented models across several brands. Some of them desperately need the funds – for example, Maserati – by the way.
While many of the Stellantis brands have already been reorganized during the FastLane 2030 and related announcements, Maserati has been left out of the business development plan because it will come with its own strategy by the end of the year. And no, we’re not talking about the recent announcement about the Maserati Island in Dubai .
Instead, the ailing luxury Italian brand is widely expected to showcase its new business strategy in December 2026 in a dedicated announcement where the rumor mill thinks we will also see fresh concepts that could preview the next Levante crossover SUV and Quattroporte four-door sedan.
Well, someone decided to jump the fence a little faster and come up with at least the latter way ahead of the official timeline – obviously, we are dealing here with a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI.
More precisely, Thibault Devauze, the Chief Designer at GAC Milano, who also has previous work experience at Audi, Land Rover, or General Motors, moonlights as a virtual artist known as ' thibaultdevauzedesign ' on social media, and crafted this Maserati GT sedan prototype as their latest unofficial, hypothetical design project.

Air cargo GSSA and broker Simple Cargo says it is handling around 30% more shipments with the same number of staff, after bringing sales, bookings, and invoicing into a single cargo management system.
The company, which operates in the Netherlands and Belgium, is the launch customer for FreightSpark ONE, and managing partner Gert-Jan Lantrok told The Loadstar automation had reduced its daily booking workload from a full working day for one employee to about an hour.
“We have the same number of people, but we are handling around 30% more shipments,” he said. “Even with that growth, ONE has given us more time, not less. We use it to give customers better service and to follow up on the things that really matter.”
Simple Cargo previously ran operations and finance in another software package, supported by spreadsheets and documents. It already used FreightSpark’s quotation tool, which has since become part of ONE.
The Belgian team switched at the start of the year, followed by the Dutch operation in July.
Mr Lantrok said the practical gains came from keeping information together throughout a shipment’s journey. Operations staff could see the original customer request, quotation, and airline confirmation in one place, while documents and correspondence remained linked to the shipment.
“When an RFQ comes in, a quote option is often already prepared, and we only have to check it and send it,” he explained.
Pre-booking and updating multiple flights could also be completed together, while incoming supplier invoices that previously required hours of printing and checking now took minutes, he said.
FreightSpark enters a market already served by companies like Awery, whose platform combines commercial, operational, and financial workflows for airlines, GSSAs, and brokers. Awery also offers eMagic to extract cargo details from emailed quotation requests and produce structured quotes.
FreightSpark founder Frank Smit argued that fragmented software was limiting what cargo businesses could achieve with AI.
“The enquiry arrives in Outlook, the quote is built in another tool, and the booking is made in a third. Finance then works from its own system,” he said. “If the data is spread across five tools, an AI agent only sees part of the picture.”
ONE carries information from enquiry through quotation, shipment and invoice. Its AI functions include extracting details from customer enquiries and air waybills, and capturing supplier invoice information for checking.
“The team stays in control: AI prepares, people review and decide,” said Mr Smit.
He said FreightSpark’s ambition was to replace legacy cargo systems. Its current customers are GSSAs and brokers, although the product is also designed to manage airlines’ own cargo operations.
Pricing is based on team size, with no per-shipment or usage-based fees, he added.
There are still tasks Simple Cargo performs elsewhere. Book-keeping remains in Exact, and some airlines require bookings through their own systems because automated connections are unavailable. The company also uses Claude for some tasks, connected to its data in ONE.
The productivity figures are Simple Cargo’s own estimates, but Mr Lantrok said the time released was going into customer service.
And when The Loadstar remarked on the speed of his email responses, he offered a more informal assessment: “Lots of spare time due to using FS ONE!”

Ford Gets Into the Spacecraft Manufacturing Business by Buying Into Revolution Space
6 photos
Photo: Ford
I remember a time, not long ago, when American carmaker Ford rolled out so many new vehicles that we, the ones covering such things, sometimes found it difficult to keep up. That time is gone now, and we all have to think pretty hard to remember how long ago a brand-new Ford came out.
In a bid to cut costs and boost profit margins, the Blue Oval decided to stick to its present range of trucks and SUVs, with the only major investment on the horizon being the upcoming Fathom family. That, and a spacecraft, it seems.
Having determined through undisclosed internal mechanisms that the space industry is the way of the future, the carmaker announced this week it has taken a minority stake in American space systems contractor Revolution Space.
These guys have been around for more than a decade now, and they are in the business of making anything from propulsion systems for spacecraft to the spacecraft (mostly satellites) itself.
Ford's participation in Revolution Space goes beyond simply throwing money at it. We are told the carmaker will apply its manufacturing expertise to scale production of an upcoming spacecraft of an undisclosed nature.
From the few details we got with this announcement, I was able to pick up a few things about this new spacecraft. There is talk of it being able to be part of constellations that do their thing in communications, navigation, and Earth observation.
There are hopes the money Ford invests in the space company (a sum that was not disclosed, paid through the carmaker's Industrial Platform LLC subsidiary) will increase Revolution's reach and allow it to place these satellites in low-Earth orbit, geosynchronous orbit, cislunar orbit, and potentially even beyond.
Ford says the move, which came a bit as a surprise, seeing how not that many carmakers turn their attention to the space exploration industry (yet), is part of a broader effort to invest in businesses that have the potential of being very profitable. And this opens the door to potentially other surprise investments in the coming years.
Just to give us a sense of what profitable means in this case, Ford cites World Economic Forum numbers that point to this industry growing from $600 billion today to $1.8 trillion by 2035.
Most of that money is to be made in the satellite business, of course. According to Future Market Insights, the satellite market was worth up to $26 billion last year, and should grow to as much as $114 billion over the next decade.
There is even a hint that, someday in the future, Ford might make satellites itself. It wouldn't be the first time the carmaker repurposed some of its assembly lines, having already produced bombers, tanks, and jeeps during the Second World War and ventilators and personal protective equipment during the pandemic.
When it comes to space exploration, the Blue Oval has been involved in it before, having produced comms and weather satellites for NASA and the armed forces in the 1960s and 1970s.
We'll keep an eye on things and report back when and if we learn anything new about Ford's renewed interest (and involvement) in space exploration.

The Kleox Move Slide-Out Teardrop Is Probably the Smallest Camping Trailer in the World
10 photos
Photo: Kleox
As popular wisdom would have it, the strongest essences are kept in the smallest of vials. This might be an old and tired cliché, but boy does it work for the new Kleox Move teardrop trailer!
The reason you have not heard of the Kleox Move before is that it doesn't exist yet.
It's still in prototype stage and it's making its big international debut as one, with aspirations as high as its dimensions are compact. The Move wants to become "what might be the world's smallest camping trailer," ultralight and super-compact, and incredibly easy to tow, maneuver, and park in the desired location.
All these promises come close to the dreaded "too good to be true" phrase, but if anything, Kleox has proven over the years that they are experts at reconciling paradoxes and delivering exactly what they promise in marketing materials. The company released the first Kleox Shelter teardrop trailer some five years ago and, just one year later, reception and strong demand already fueled a new iteration and model.
Photo: Kleox From day one, though, the Kleox teardrop was designed as what the name implies: a basic shelter on wheels. It was never meant to be one of those fancy teardrops that promise to be pint-sized houses on wheels and let alone resemble the bigger caravans that allow to pack most of the creature comforts onboard.
Part of the reason why the Kleox Shelter was so popular was that it was imagined from the get-go as a hybrid between a tent and a trailer, with the possibility to double as a cargo trailer when you weren't taking it out on vacation. It wasn't just an RV, though that would have been enough for most buyers, but it was also something you could use in your everyday life, with minimal effort on your part to get from one mode to the other.
This approach survived as popularity and demand increased. Today, Kleox is offering two models of the Kleox teardrop, all designed to be basic solutions for camping with extra utility in everyday life and a price point that won't have you running for the hills.
Photo: Kleox They are the Kleox Shelter Travel and the Kleox Festival. A Kleox Shelter Basic is also available , but that's just an empty shell, so Kleox doesn't count it as a proper model. The Move will be joining the family as "the third Musketeer" hopefully by Q3 of 2028, though no sooner than Q2 of that same year.
Unlike its older siblings, the Move is a slide-out model that will offer a more compact form factor and a lighter weight for an extra dose of convenience. As I said, big dreams for such a little thing.
The first photos of the prototype reveal a slide-out unit with shell-in-shell design, where the forward shell slides out of the bigger one once you arrive at camp. This allows the teardrop to travel surprisingly small and expand at camp with a simple, swift push forward. Kleox says it will still offer sleeping for two adults inside, so the expansion will be considerable.
Photo: Kleox In terms of dimensions , Kleox says that Move will come in at just 2.65 meters (8.7 feet) of total length, so it will be smaller than the 3.20-meter (10.5-foot) Travel or Festival models. It will also be 15 cm (5.9 inches) shorter than these for even better aerodynamics.
At camp, it will offer 205 cm (80.7 inches) of floor length, Kleox tells New Atlas, so it sounds like it could, indeed, fit two adults comfortably . The chassis and tongue are fixed, so the Move will tow easily even on winding roads, Kleox explains for the same media outlet.
In terms of build and design, the Move will be just like its older and beefier siblings. That means a single-axle unbraked AL-KO chassis and a fiberglass body with a felted interior for insulation and improved acoustics.
Photo: Kleox Another thing the three will have in common will be the extra functionality as a transport slash enclosed cargo trailer. The other Kleox models can be purchased with minimal equipment that will take a minimal amount of time to remove to use the trailer for hauling stuff, and it seems like this is the plan for the Move as well.
Of course, given the fact that it will be smaller, the Move will probably fit less stuff inside, whether standard or add-ons. Not that you can pack too much, either way: a foldable mattress, a few more netted pockets, a little shelf, a reading light, that kind of stuff.
The same media outlet notes that Kleox hopes to keep the weight of the Move below 250 kg (551 lbs) or perhaps as low as 227 kg (500 lbs).
Photo: Kleox Since we're on the topic of hopeful thinking, Kleox is eyeing a physical debut of a more polished prototype for the 2027 Dusseldorf Caravan Salon, which will take place at the end of next August. However, they're setting that as a soft target date, acknowledging that progress on this new model hasn't been as smooth as they anticipated.
There's no word on pricing yet. The Travel and Festival models start at €6,590 now, which is approximately $7,200 at the current exchange rate, so it would stand to reason for Move to be cheaper.
Right now, Kleox is taking feedback on the first prototype. They're also welcoming suggestions for a final name: the trailer is tentatively called Move, with the other option being the Kleox Flex.

source_document.body:
The perceived threat of Most Favored Nation drug pricing is keeping many companies out of international markets. But for some medicines, the costs of delaying entry run high.
Biotech executives will routinely risk $200 million on a priority review voucher to shave six months off a U.S. timeline, fully aware that the drug may still be rejected. Yet when it comes to international commercialization, that risk appetite vanishes. Encouraged by conservative lawyers and consultants, leadership teams are putting global launches on ice over global pricing concerns.
As CEO of Er-Kim, which partners with biotechs to bring their products to international markets, it’s clear to me that this is an irrational double standard that is burning through finite commercial windows and destroying asset value. President Donald Trump’s Most Favored Nation (MFN), which ties what U.S. programs pay for a drug to the lower prices paid in other developed countries, is not a reason to limit the value of innovative medicines.
The real cost of waiting
For biotechs, the fear under this burgeoning MFN paradigm is simple: Accept a lower launch price in one foreign market, and you risk handing U.S. payers a lower benchmark to price against.
The U.S. accounts for just over half of worldwide pharmaceutical spending. If ex-U.S. markets are not pursued, stateside business must roughly double—whether in terms of volume or price or, most likely, a mix of both—to preserve the same peak revenue. For some products, the international contribution is substantially larger. Ex-U.S. markets represented approximately 73% of the achondroplasia market in 2025, for example.
What is the likelihood that the lost ex-U.S. revenue can be recouped within the country? This is the missing question in many MFN discussions. The risk to U.S. pricing is examined extensively, while the revenue sacrificed outside the country is treated as though it carries no cost.
The real choice is not between international risk and no risk, but between two distinct risks: the effect of international pricing on the U.S. business versus the value lost by delaying ex-U.S. expansion.
Drug pricing
Trump’s MFN Pricing Expected To Delay More European Drug Launches
Following Insmed’s decision to hold off on launching a newly approved lung disease drug in Europe, experts anticipate more companies will do the same as they seek to avoid price erosion in the U.S. Will Chinese biotechs fill the void?
April 1, 2026
·
3 min read
·
Nick Paul Taylor
Read more
A medicine is strictly a time-limited asset, its economic life defined by patent windows and influenced by competitive erosion. Delay—a less extreme form of abandonment—may preserve optionality, but it also pushes international cash flows further into the future while the asset’s remaining commercial life declines.
Sometimes that commercial life is shorter than executives expect. The head start for first-mover therapies in the rare disease space is shrinking at a rapid pace, with pioneer treatments now often facing swift competition.
In spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), Biogen’s Spinraza was approved in December 2016. Novartis’ Zolgensma followed approximately 29 months later, and Roche’s Evrysdi 14 months after that. In under four years, SMA went from zero approved therapies to three. In hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Akcea’s Tegsedi followed Alnylam’s Onpattro by just 56 days. And for Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC), IntraBio’s Agneursa came only four days after Zevra Therapeutics’ Miplyffa in September 2024, with three more NPC therapies already filed with the FDA or currently in Phase 3.
These fast-follower launches underscore why delaying a commercial rollout is a high-stakes strategic decision that requires the same rigorous analytical evaluation as a major capital investment.
A more rational approach
Some leadership teams appear to be waiting for the political winds in Washington to shift before making a call on international launch plans. That is a miscalculation.
Bipartisan momentum behind government drug price negotiations—from President Trump’s MFN executive orders to Democratic Medicare price negotiation frameworks—signals a shift. Sticking to an “all eggs in one basket” strategy by relying 100% on U.S. sales leaves biotechs exposed. If U.S. price negotiations accelerate and a company does not have an international footprint, it is left with zero market leverage and no secondary revenue streams to buffer the impact.
The American public supports government intervention in drug pricing. In a recent KFF Tracking Poll on Health Information and Trust, 59% of U.S. adults said they were worried about affording prescription medicines—the highest level since tracking began in 2018. Seventy-two percent, including 68% of Republicans, said there is insufficient government regulation of drug prices.
Caution is not risk management—it is the refusal to manage risk.
Furthermore, a separate KFF poll found 84% of Americans agree that U.S. patients pay higher prices than those in other countries, and that many cannot afford their prescriptions and believe drug company profits are too high. The industry’s counterargument, that government involvement means fewer new drugs, convinces just 33% of respondents.
This public sentiment suggests that whichever way the political winds may blow, a rollback of price oversight is highly unlikely. Threatening to withhold drugs or pull out of international markets to preserve U.S. pricing power has already proven unsuccessful in Europe, and could prove even less effective as U.S. price controls expand.
But ex-U.S. pricing is far from uniform. In some markets, competition is compressing prices in certain therapeutic areas, while severe unmet need and limited budget impact support materially higher prices in others. Treating every international market as a uniform pricing risk obscures the differences that a rational launch strategy should exploit.
The relevant decision, therefore, is not whether to launch internationally, but when, where and under what contractual protections. The geography of value is drug-specific. Some rare disease products derive most of their treatable population and commercial opportunity from international markets; other assets may remain heavily concentrated in high-premium U.S. channels. Management’s first task is to establish where the asset sits on that spectrum.
Once the exposure is quantified and a company has a realistic view of global pricing risks, leaders can protect asset value while still expanding internationally by:
Staging the order in which a drug is launched in various countries based on how those regions influence prices in other regions.
Rethinking an ex-U.S. footprint centered on downstream risk mitigation. Managing commercial exposure means avoiding strict, high-cost investments early in a launch. Establishing flexible market access frameworks allows companies to maintain better oversight over global pricing and negotiations while bypassing the heavy overhead of dedicated local sales forces.
Designing flexible partnerships by structuring deal terms so that when entering key markets, companies are not locking themselves into permanent pricing commitments that may not work out down the line.
International commercialization should not be treated as an all-or-nothing hazard. It is a standard, model-able business risk. Waiting may ultimately prove to be the correct decision in specific cases, but it can only be called rational after the value preserved by waiting has been weighed against the discounted international revenue, competitive positioning and remaining commercial life being surrendered.
Biotech leaders routinely make decisions under profound scientific uncertainty. International commercialization deserves the same courage and discipline. Until both sides of the equation have been quantified, caution is not risk management—it is the refusal to manage risk.

By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
24 November 2026
Mexico’s premier Pacific gateway is moving closer to a massive expansion after the national environmental agency gave its conditional approval for the first phase of the Puerto Nuevo Manzanillo project.
This is a M$118.39bn (US$6.26bn) initiative to boost the port’s operating area from 450ha to more than 1,880ha and triple its container throughput capacity.
The Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources approved a revised proposal by Asipona Manzanillo, the port administration, after the original submission had been closed last December.
Work on phase one, which should take about six years, is expected to commence in January and will see the creation of platforms for two container terminals and navigation channels. The second phase, if approved, would commence in January 2049, adding two more box terminals and a multi-use facility, and expand the rail infrastructure.
The project has the backing of the administration in Mexico City, which is eager to expand the nation’s transpacific trade, after the Pacific gateways clocked up record growth this year. Manzanillo, the nation’s largest container port, saw throughput rise nearly 10% in the first half, to 2.07m teu, and for the first nine months, the port registered close to 3.16m teu, up 9.5% year on year.
Lazaro Cardenas, Mexico’s second-largest Pacific cargo gateway, saw box volume climb 7% in the January-September period, to almost 1.58m teu, while tonnage jumped 14% to 17.48m tonnes.
And traffic looks set to continue to increase in the new year. Hapag Lloyd announced two new services between Asia and Latin America last week for the coming year. The first, scheduled to launch in January, will be the Asia-Mexico Express, a weekly operation using panamax vessels from Ningbo and Qingdao via Busan to Ensenada, Manzanillo, and Lazaro Cardenas, with transits from Mexican ports to destinations on the west coast of Latin America.
The other new service, scheduled for April, will serve ports on South America’s east coast.
This month, Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum led a government delegation to the APEC summit in Guangzhou, aiming to develop and grow commercial ties with Asian nations. Talks included a meeting with Chinese officials and produced an agreement to set up a working group to explore mechanisms to bolster Mexican exports to China, primarily agricultural.
According to Marcelo Ebrard, Mexico’s secretary of economy, China’s exports to Mexico will exceed $130bn this year, whereas trade in the opposite direction is just $10bn.

Insmed will bolster Sanofi’s immunology and inflammation portfolio, which is currently led by Regeneron-partnered blockbuster Dupixent.
Sanofi’s new CEO Belen Garijo certainly knows how to make a first impression. Just shy of seven full months in the role, Garijo has struck biopharma’s largest M&A deal of the year, with the French pharma offering $41 billion in cash for rare disease and immunology company Insmed.
Insmed will bolster Sanofi’s immunology and inflammation portfolio, which is currently led by Regeneron-partnered blockbuster Dupixent.
Stars of the acquisition are Insmed’s approved products Brinsupri for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFB) and Arikayce, an inhaled therapy for mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease. Insmed also has a deep pipeline of therapies in respiratory disease, I&I, neurological disease and rare disease.

Only Jeep Wrangler Commando 392 Not Meant for Soldiers and Veterans Sells for $174,000
10 photos
Photo: Jeep
Earlier in November, American carmaker Jeep announced an exclusive production run of the Jeep Wrangler Commando 392. The fine print was that all but one of the 250 units to be made were not meant for the general public, but for active-duty military personnel and veterans, who had to register their interest for a chance to get one.
We don't know how that's going, except for the fact that some 4,700 applications have been submitted, meaning every single person is going head-to-head against 18 other people for the chance of owning one of these special SUVs. We do know, however, what happened to the 250th Commando 392 .
As stated ever since the limited edition was announced, the final vehicle of this run was to go under the hammer in an online auction hosted by Bring a Trailer. The auction gates opened on November 11 and closed this weekend, on November 22.
At the end of it all, the winner committed to paying $174,000 for the honor of owning the only Jeep Wrangler Commando 392 meant for the general public. For reference, the Wrangler 392 in its most basic, standard form starts at more than half that at the time of writing, $69,995.
Except for the fact that this particular trail-rated SUV is the last in its production run, there are no special fittings setting it apart from its 249 siblings meant for service members and veterans. Based on the Wrangler 392 platform, it was modified with assistance from factory-upfitted truck specialist Fox.
We are not told exactly what kind of Fox suspension system is used in this application, but it ties into custom wheels shod in massive, 37-inch tires that move under the power supplied by the base SUV's engine, the 6.4-liter V8.
Other than the fitting of the fancier suspension system, the 392 comes with no changes to its powertrain and performance levels. There are, however, plenty of visual upgrades meant to set it apart from the standard version, including exclusive graphics and unique badging.
The Jeep's overall look, with its military-inspired appearance, is meant to remind the world of the brand's past involvement with the military, but also of the Jeepster Commando after which it was named. Inside, there is word of custom modifications centered around one-of-one colors and trim treatments.
The $174,000 someone paid for this ride won't go to Jeep, or Fox , and not even Bring a Trailer. This was a charity auction, meant to support the United Service Organizations (USO), and that's where all the money will go.
USO is a congressionally chartered 501(c)(3) nonprofit focused on providing morale, welfare, and recreation services to members of the U.S. Armed Forces and their families – naturally, the money from this sale will be used to advance the organization's programs.

There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.
These days, apparently those are rookie numbers.
Spend enough time browsing new e-bike launches and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power. Dual-motor models have turned the spec sheet into an arms race, with manufacturers seemingly competing to see who can slap the biggest number onto the product page.
If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
To be clear, I’m not anti-power. I’ve ridden everything from dainty 250W European commuter bikes to electric motorcycles with enough power to rearrange your chest cavity. Powerful electric two-wheelers are fun, period.
But there’s a difference between building a powerful electric two-wheeler and pretending that every powerful electric two-wheeler is still an electric bicycle.
In the US, the widely adopted three-class e-bike system generally tops out at 20 mph (32 km/h) for Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes and 28 mph (45 km/h) for Class 3, with some minor exceptions, and 750 watts has long been a common benchmark for the motor power limit.
Yet browse online e-bike retailers today and you’ll find plenty of machines advertised with motors well beyond that figure, often capable of speeds far beyond normal electric bicycle classifications.
Sometimes there’s a disclaimer explaining that the bike is intended for “off-road use.” Sometimes there’s a software setting that supposedly limits it for street riding.
And sometimes people just sort of squint at the pedals and agree to keep calling it an electric bicycle.
The problem isn’t that 2,000W electric two-wheelers exist. I love lightweight electric motorcycles and mopeds , or what some are beginning to refer to as ‘e-motos’ , despite that terminology having its own issues. So sure, those bikes are great and there is a time and place for such power. The problem is that the industry increasingly seems afraid to call them what they are.
Part of the blame belongs to consumers – to us.
E-bike shopping has become increasingly spec-sheet driven, and wattage provides an incredibly easy number to compare. If ‘Bike A’ has a 750W motor and ‘Bike B’ costs the same but advertises 1,500W, it’s easy to assume ‘Bike B’ is twice as good. This is especially true for younger riders who lack a deeper understanding of how e-bikes work, and just want something powerful and fast to impress their friends after school. They beg their parents for the latest models with the biggest motors, and many parents give in.
The problem is that’s not how electric bikes work – there’s so much more to a bike than the motor wattage rating.
Motor design, controller current, battery voltage, thermal management, gearing, efficiency and software tuning all influence performance. A beautifully tuned 500W or 750W system can be far nicer to ride – and sometimes more useful – than a poorly implemented motor advertising twice the power.
But “excellent controller tuning” doesn’t look nearly as exciting in a giant font on an Amazon listing. So manufacturers respond rationally based on what consumers demand: They make the number bigger.
The result is an e-bike horsepower war that is ultimately hurting the entire industry.
When riders blast through bike paths on motorcycle-performance machines marketed as “e-bikes,” pedestrians don’t care whether the motor technically arrived in a street-legal mode. Police officers aren’t going to inspect controller settings. And lawmakers aren’t famous for approaching emerging transportation technology with surgical precision.
They see a fast machine with pedals, hear complaints about dangerous “e-bikes,” and start writing laws that affect everyone – including riders on perfectly ordinary commuter e-bikes.
In my opinion, that’s the part that should worry anyone who enjoys riding an e-bike.
There’s absolutely a place for high-powered electric two-wheelers. In fact, I want more of them. Lightweight electric mopeds and motorcycles could replace an enormous number of car trips while using a fraction of the energy and space. Those are highly capable machines, but they need to be used appropriately, registered legally, and ridden responsibly.
And we don’t help that cause by pretending they’re bicycles.
Perhaps the e-bike industry’s next great innovation doesn’t need another 500 watts.
Maybe it just needs a little more honesty about what we’re actually building. So let’s build more electric bicycles. And yes, let’s build more e-motos and electric motorcycles. But let’s not confuse the two, either.

Go Mango 1970 Dodge Super Bee Has Seen Better Days, Needs Second Chance
14 photos
Photo: nicomedes99/eBay
In 1968, both Dodge and Plymouth introduced entry-level muscle cars on the B-body architecture. These cars hit showrooms as the Super Bee and Road Runner , respectively. Although they were largely similar, one was significantly more popular than the other.
The Road Runner was the most desirable of the two, selling over 180,000 units through 1971. The Super Bee, on the other hand, only moved about 56,000 examples over the same period. While the Road Runner returned in 1972, the Super Bee went into the history books when Chrysler discontinued its high-compression V8 engines.
What's with the massive gap, given that these vehicles were similar and came with nearly identical options? Well, most historians speculate that it may have something to do with pricing. While the Road Runner came in at $2,870 in 1968, the Super Bee started from $3,027. I guess many enthusiasts weren't willing to pay the 5% premium to get the Super Bee.
Whatever the case, these figures make the Super Bee the rarer classic today. The 1970 hardtop you see here, for instance, is one of 15,506 units sold that year. For reference, Plymouth sold over 40,000 Road Runners. The body style, by the way, narrows its production number to 11,540 examples.
Yes, this Mopar is far from super rare by production figures alone, but it was born in a relatively rare and desirable color. I'm talking about Go Mango, one of the 10 high-impact colors. Called Vitamin C on Plymouth models, Go Mango was only available for two model years, 1969 and 1970. It also has the white bumblebee stripe and white interior, for an even rarer combo.
Unfortunately, this Super Bee is in pretty bad shape. It's unclear how it ended up like this, but it looks like it's been sitting for a few decades. The paint is badly weathered, much of the bumblebee stripe is gone, while the interior is quite dirty and missing the original driver's seat. The numbers-matching engine is also gone.
It still has a mill under the hood, but it's not original to this car. However, it's a 383-cubic-inch (6.3-liter) V8, just like the original powerplant. The big-block unit came standard in the Super Bee in 1970. It's paired with a three-speed TorqueFlite automatic, which makes for a very common combo.
The Mopar spent most of its life in California, so it's pretty much rust-free. The seller claims that the vehicle is 90% complete in terms of parts. There's no word on whether the EK2 Go Mango paint is original, but it sure looks like it.
Overall, this 1970 Super Bee is a super solid project and a muscle car that deserves a second chance. The car is in Santa Ana, California, and the seller wants $17,500 or the best offer to let it go. Is it worth restoring?
